The crinoline is a stiffened petticoat or hoop skirt made of horsehair fabric or flexible steel hoops, worn primarily from the eighteen fifty through eighteen eighties to create a full, bell-shaped silhouette. Cheaper and more flexible than the rigid farthingale of earlier centuries, the crinoline became the defining understructure of Victorian fashion, creating the iconic wide skirts that defined an entire era.

Originally a stiff fabric made from horsehair and linen—the word crin means horsehair—which was bulky but effective, it was later replaced by flexible steel hoops that were lighter and more comfortable. The steel-hoop crinoline, patented in eighteen fifty-six, revolutionized construction by allowing wearers to achieve extreme width—skirts could exceed six feet in circumference—with relative flexibility. At its peak around eighteen sixty, the crinoline was so wide that women struggled to pass through doorways, sit in carriages, or navigate stairs. The silhouette was functionally impractical but fashionable beyond utility.

Worn in layers, typically three to five petticoats were layered over the crinoline frame, with the outermost skirt draped and trimmed to create volume and silhouette. The crinoline democratized fashionable silhouette. Cheaper than elaborate tailoring, it allowed middle-class women to approximate aristocratic width and status. However, the garment was subject to serious safety hazards. Crinolines were dangerously flammable, and women routinely suffered burns from candles and fires catching the skirt. Crinoline-related accidents were common causes of injury.

The garment gradually declined in the eighteen seventies and eighties as the bustle redirected volume toward the rear, and modern fashion movements began rejecting extreme silhouettes. The crinoline shares its story with the farthingale, the earlier hooped understructure that created similar dramatic silhouettes, and the corset, the rigid companion garment worn with crinolines to create the Victorian hourglass ideal. The bustle emerged as the successor garment that replaced the full crinoline skirt with rear projection. The garment's dominance was cemented during the reign of Victoria, the British queen during the peak of crinoline fashion and dominance.
